title: Feature request: Obtain the list of blocks in a snapshot

Output of `restic version`

restic 0.18.0 compiled with go1.24.1 on darwin/amd64
<!--
Please add the version of restic you're currently using here, this helps us
later to see what has changed in restic when we revisit this issue after some
time.
-->

What should restic do differently? Which functionality do you think we should add?
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Have a way to list the blocks present in a snapshot; even better, the blocks in a snapshot in a file path

An alternative would be a way to try to read fist few bytes in a block and report a list of failures (which would save a lot of time as well).

<!--
Please describe the feature you'd like us to add here.
-->


What are you trying to do? What problem would this solve?
---------------------------------------------------------
We keep all backups in AWS S3. We have a lifecycle policy to transition to IA after 90 days and to DEEP_ARCHIVE after 390 days.

The deduplication feature is awesome, but it is really annoying when trying to provide developers with a 3 weeks old backup and you notice 2, 3 maybe 9 blocks in that backup are in DEEP_ARCHIVE.

The only way to do it is to attempt a restore, capture all those 

```
Load(<data/7f7096ecc6>, 1362710, 3273655) returned error, retrying after 1m3.303469605s: The operation is not valid for the object's storage class
```

then make a unique list of failed block ids and feed the list into a glacier restore script.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant1, thank you for the link. This sounds interesting. I am testing it now (which might take quite a bit).
In the mean time I do have some questions.

How does restic manages a restore operation where there are like 10 data blocks in Glacier and the rest in Standard storage class?  Will it find out about the blocks in Glacier and issue a restoration request? Or the restoration request for the second data block would only be issued after the first one is being successfully restored? 

Sounds dumb, but I do want to make sure I don't wait for <glacier blocks count> x <average glacier restore time ~ 12h> for the restore to complete.

I think the most sensible way would be to try to do a normal restore until we hit a data block stored in glacier; a glacier restore request should be issued but then I think restic should go through the rest of the data blocks as fast as possible, sending glacier restore requests where required and exit early, stating that for X blocks (maybe the list attached) a glacier request has been sent and that we should run it again after X hours (say 12 hours).

I think that would be preferable than keeping `restic restore` running for some unspecified amount of time. 

It might be that I didn't understood the process very well though.

Tagging @participant2 who would be probably the most capable to explain the behaviour.

Thank you for your work!

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Can't tell for sure from your logs, but I assume it tries to read from tree blobs that should be hot but are actually not (probably because of your transition policy). See https://github.com/restic/restic/issues/3202#issuecomment-2848803839 to restore them first. `restic restore` may work after that.

> We have a lifecycle policy to transition to IA after 90 days and to DEEP_ARCHIVE after 390 days.

This is not supported. You must remove the lifecycle policy and restore all tree blobs first. `s3.enable-restore` will only work well when using `-o s3.storage-class=GLACIER` or `-o s3.storage-class=DEEP_ARCHIVE` during backups and nothing else. FAQ should maybe be clearer about that.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: Since I down know how AWS S3 works, I have to rely on @reporter to tell me if this works for you. I hope that all tree blobs reside in an AWS storage type which is quickly accessible. This command relies on the being able to read all tree blobs.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant3, thank you for your work! 🎉 
It looks like it is working just fine, with both long and short IDs.
The automatic lifecycle we have in AWS S3 only affects the files stored in the `/data` directory for the restic repository, while the other things (like `/index`) will stay in the standard storage.
Being able to use your new command enabled me to save a lot of time, since I don't need to actually try a restore that will most likely fail just to obtain the short IDs for the data that is not in the standard storage anymore. With you commanf, I am able to get the complete list of the data IDs used in the snapshot and feed the list through a script that will check which is not in the standard storage and initiate the procedure to bring it back to standard storage for 7 days.
Looking forward to see your work merged in the main restic! 🚀 

Will close this, hoping the changes will make it to new release.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: Make sure that the metadata, which also live in the /data subdirectory will be kept in standard storage. When using the `packfilelist command` with option `--detail=1`, you will see the metadata packfiles marked as "tree". The `packfilelist` command reads these metadata packfiles and builds the set `usedBlobs`, which is the set of all blobs ("data" and "tree") used in this snapshot.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: I think the metadata is stored within the `keys` and `config` directories, no?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
You are correct. I was able to replicate your example. Thank you for that.

So in my case, having the `/data` directory partially into Glacier, but having `/index`, `/config`, `/keys`, `/snapshots` in normal storage, would put me in a position to not be able to list all the blocks used by a snapshot?

My simpleton understanding would be that I could get from index what I need to get lower and lower to the actual data blocks (metadata, tree, etc).

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> So in my case, having the /data directory partially into Glacier, but having /index, /config, /keys, /snapshots in normal storage, would put me in a position to not be able to list all the blocks used by a snapshot?

Yes you need all of /index, /config, /keys, /snapshots in normal storage. In addition, all the metadata packfiles, which you can get from 
``restic packfilelist --all --detail| grep tree`` have also to be in normal storage to guarantee that the ``packfilelist`` command can run without getting stuck in Glacier.

See also https://restic.readthedocs.io/en/stable/100_references.html#trees-and-data. There it is explained how a tree actually looks like.
